title: Getting Started with mapycusmaximus
text: mapycusmaximus brings fisheye transformations R’s spatial ecosystem. Just ggplot2 transforms visualize data dplyr transforms manipulate , mapycusmaximus transforms view geographic space—allowing magnify local detail preserving regional context. package implements Focus-Glue-Context (FGC) model, three-zone radial transformation : Magnifies features focus region (like zooming ) Smoothly transitions glue zone (preventing jarring distortions) Preserves outer context (maintaining geographic orientation) vignette show use mapycusmaximus real spatial data, following tidyverse principles working data.
code: library(mapycusmaximus) library(sf) library(ggplot2)  # Use a minimal theme for clean visualizations theme_set(theme_minimal())

title: Getting Started with mapycusmaximus
text: Let’s start built-Victoria LGA dataset. goal magnify Melbourne keeping rest Victoria visible. simplest fisheye uses defaults automatically determines center: basic fisheye transformation Victoria’s LGAs ’s ! really control transformation, ’ll want specify focus point.
code: # Examine the data data(vic) vic #> Simple feature collection with 79 features and 1 field #> Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON #> Dimension:     XY #> Bounding box:  xmin: 140.9619 ymin: -39.13442 xmax: 149.9762 ymax: -33.98064 #> Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84 #> First 10 features: #>      LGA_NAME                       geometry #> 1      ALPINE MULTIPOLYGON (((146.7238 -3... #> 2      ARARAT MULTIPOLYGON (((143.0904 -3... #> 3    BALLARAT MULTIPOLYGON (((143.9239 -3... #> 4     BANYULE MULTIPOLYGON (((145.1342 -3... #> 5  BASS COAST MULTIPOLYGON (((145.3214 -3... #> 6     BAW BAW MULTIPOLYGON (((145.7643 -3... #> 7     BAYSIDE MULTIPOLYGON (((144.986 -37... #> 8     BENALLA MULTIPOLYGON (((146.1131 -3... #> 9  BOROONDARA MULTIPOLYGON (((145.1039 -3... #> 10   BRIMBANK MULTIPOLYGON (((144.8829 -3... # Apply fisheye transformation vic_warped <- sf_fisheye(   vic,   r_in = 0.3,        # Focus radius   r_out = 0.6,       # Glue boundary   zoom_factor = 2,   # Magnification strength   squeeze_factor = 0.35 )  # Visualize with ggplot2 ggplot(vic_warped) +   geom_sf(fill = "grey90", color = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +   labs(title = "Victoria LGAs with Default Fisheye")

title: Getting Started with mapycusmaximus
text: fisheye center determines gets magnified. several ways specify :

title: Getting Started with mapycusmaximus
text: natural approach—pass sf object mapycusmaximus uses centroid: Fisheye centered Melbourne CBD
code: # Extract Melbourne CBD as the focus melbourne <- vic[vic$LGA_NAME == "MELBOURNE", ]  vic_melbourne <- sf_fisheye(   vic,   center = melbourne,      # Centroid becomes the warp center   r_in = 0.34,   r_out = 0.60,   zoom_factor = 15,   squeeze_factor = 0.35 )  ggplot() +   geom_sf(data = vic_melbourne, fill = "grey92", color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +   geom_sf(data = melbourne, fill = NA, color = "tomato", linewidth = 0.8) +   labs(title = "Melbourne CBD Magnified",        subtitle = "Focus defined by Melbourne LGA geometry")

title: Getting Started with mapycusmaximus
text: multiple layers (points, lines, polygons), transform together ensure alignment: Multiple aligned layers fisheye transformation combine first? layers transformed separately, may different bounding boxes, leading slightly different normalized coordinates misalignment.
code: # Create centroids as a point layer centroids <- st_centroid(vic)  # Add a layer identifier to each vic_layer <- vic |>    dplyr::mutate(layer = "polygon")  centroids_layer <- centroids |>    dplyr::mutate(layer = "centroid")  # Combine layers before transformation both_layers <- rbind(   vic_layer[, c("LGA_NAME", "geometry", "layer")],   centroids_layer[, c("LGA_NAME", "geometry", "layer")] )  # Apply fisheye once to combined data both_warped <- sf_fisheye(   both_layers,   center = melbourne,   r_in = 0.34,   r_out = 0.60,   zoom_factor = 12,   squeeze_factor = 0.35 )  # Separate for plotting polygons_warped <- both_warped[both_warped$layer == "polygon", ] points_warped <- both_warped[both_warped$layer == "centroid", ]  # Plot together ggplot() +   geom_sf(data = polygons_warped, fill = "grey92", color = "white",            linewidth = 0.2) +   geom_sf(data = points_warped, color = "#2b6cb0", size = 1.2, alpha = 0.7) +   labs(title = "Aligned Layers: Polygons and Centroids",        subtitle = "Transformed together to ensure perfect alignment")

title: Getting Started with mapycusmaximus
text: mapycusmaximus projection-aware handles CRS transformations automatically:

title: Getting Started with mapycusmaximus
text: data longitude/latitude, package automatically selects appropriate projected CRS: package uses sensible defaults: - Victoria region → EPSG:7855 (GDA2020 / MGA Zone 55) - areas → UTM zones based centroid
code: # Create data in WGS84 vic_lonlat <- st_transform(vic, "EPSG:4326") st_crs(vic_lonlat)$proj4string #> [1] "+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84 +no_defs"  # Apply fisheye - auto-projects to GDA2020/MGA55 for Victoria vic_auto <- sf_fisheye(   vic_lonlat,   center = melbourne,   r_in = 0.3,   r_out = 0.5,   zoom_factor = 10,   squeeze_factor = 0.35 )  # Original CRS is restored st_crs(vic_auto)$proj4string #> [1] "+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84 +no_defs"

title: Getting Started with mapycusmaximus
text: ’s complete workflow showing emphasize metro area maintaining state context: Complete workflow: Metropolitan Melbourne Victorian context
code: # 1. Define the metropolitan region metro_lgas <- c("MELBOURNE", "PORT PHILLIP", "STONNINGTON", "YARRA",                  "MARIBYRNONG", "MOONEE VALLEY", "BOROONDARA",                  "GLEN EIRA", "BAYSIDE")  metro_region <- vic[vic$LGA_NAME %in% metro_lgas, ] metro_center <- st_union(metro_region) |> st_centroid()  # 2. Add a population indicator (example) vic_pop <- vic |>    dplyr::mutate(is_metro = LGA_NAME %in% metro_lgas)  # 3. Apply fisheye vic_focused <- sf_fisheye(   vic_pop,   center = metro_center,   r_in = 0.25,   r_out = 0.40,   zoom_factor = 12,   squeeze_factor = 0.35 )  # 4. Create publication-ready plot ggplot(vic_focused) +   geom_sf(aes(fill = is_metro), color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +   scale_fill_manual(     values = c("TRUE" = "#d95f02", "FALSE" = "grey85"),     labels = c("Metropolitan", "Regional"),     name = NULL   ) +   theme_minimal() +   theme(     legend.position = c(0.85, 0.15),     legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "grey70"),     panel.grid = element_blank()   ) +   labs(     title = "Metropolitan Melbourne with Regional Context",     subtitle = "Fisheye magnification preserves spatial relationships",     caption = "Transformation: r_in = 0.25, r_out = 0.40, zoom = 12"   )

title: Focus-Glue-Context Fisheye Transformations for Spatial Visualization
text: mapycusmaximus provides geometric transformations spatial planar data inspired focus–context visualization principles. package implements Focus–Glue–Context (FGC) model, enlarges region interest (focus), smoothly compresses surroundings (glue), preserves outer region (context). transformations facilitate detailed local inspection maintaining overall spatial structure.

title: Focus-Glue-Context Fisheye Transformations for Spatial Visualization
text: Fisheye transformations well-established approach visualizing dense data without losing context (Furnas 1986; Sarkar & Brown 1992).mapycusmaximus extends principles modern spatial data workflows R, integrating seamlessly sf ecosystem ggplot2 visualization grammar.

title: Focus-Glue-Context Fisheye Transformations for Spatial Visualization
text: Focus–Glue–Context transformation: smooth magnification, transition, preservation spatial zones. Full integration sf: works directly geometries automatically manages CRS transformation. Flexible centers: numeric, geographic (EPSG:4326), normalized, centroid-based. Customizable parameters: control zoom, squeeze, optional angular twist (revolution). Visualization utilities: compare original transformed coordinates plot_fisheye_fgc(). Efficient implementation: vectorized operations safe polygon re-closure.

title: Apply Focus–Glue–Context Fisheye Transformation — fisheye_fgc
text: coords matrix data frame least two columns representing x y coordinates. cx, cy Numeric. x y coordinates fisheye center (default = 0, 0). r_in Numeric. Radius focus zone (default = 0.34). r_out Numeric. Radius glue zone boundary (default = 0.5). zoom_factor Numeric. Expansion factor applied within focus zone (default = 1.5). squeeze_factor Numeric (0,1]. Compression factor applied within glue zone (smaller values = stronger compression, default = 0.3). method Character. "expand" "outward" (default = "expand"). revolution Numeric. Optional rotation factor applied glue zone. Positive values rotate counter-clockwise, negative values clockwise (default = 0.0).

title: Apply Focus–Glue–Context Fisheye Transformation — fisheye_fgc
text: numeric matrix two columns (x_new, y_new) transformed coordinates. Additional attributes: "zones": character vector classifying point "focus", "glue", "context". "original_radius": numeric vector original radial distances. "new_radius": numeric vector transformed radial distances.

title: Apply Focus–Glue–Context Fisheye Transformation — fisheye_fgc
text: function operates three radial zones around chosen center: Focus zone (r <= r_in): expands distances center using zoom_factor, exceed r_in boundary. Glue zone (r_in < r <= r_out): compresses distances using power-law defined squeeze_factor, remaps smoothly connect focus context zones. Context zone (r > r_out): coordinates remain unchanged. Optionally, points glue zone can rotated (revolution) emphasize continuity.

title: Apply Focus–Glue–Context Fisheye Transformation — fisheye_fgc

what: Radial fisheye warp for sf/sfc objects (auto-CRS + flexible centers) — sf_fisheye
title: Radial fisheye warp for sf/sfc objects (auto-CRS + flexible centers) — sf_fisheye
text: sf_fisheye() applies focus–glue–context fisheye vector data: (1) ensures sensible projected working CRS, (2) normalizes coordinates around chosen center, (3) calls fisheye_fgc() warp radii, (4) denormalizes back map units, (5) restores original CRS. Inside focus ring (r_in) features enlarge; across glue ring (r_out) transition smoothly; outside, stay nearly unchanged.

title: Radial fisheye warp for sf/sfc objects (auto-CRS + flexible centers) — sf_fisheye
text: sf_obj sf sfc object. Supports POINT, LINESTRING, POLYGON, MULTIPOLYGON. Empty geometries removed processing. center Flexible center specification (see Center selection): numeric length-2 pair interpreted via center_crs lon/lat heuristic, map units lon/lat; sf/sfc geometry, centroid derived; normalized \([-1,1]\) pair normalized_center = TRUE. center_crs Optional CRS numeric center (e.g., "EPSG:4326"). Ignored center sf/sfc object (CRS used). normalized_center Logical. TRUE, center treated normalized \([-1,1]\) coordinate around bbox midpoint. cx, cy Optional center working CRS map units (legacy path, ignored center provided). r_in, r_out Numeric radii (normalized units) defining focus glue boundaries; must satisfy r_out > r_in. zoom_factor Numeric (> 1 enlarge). Focus magnification passed fisheye_fgc(). squeeze_factor Numeric [0, 1]. Glue-zone compression strength passed fisheye_fgc(). method Character; name understood fisheye_fgc() (default "expand"). revolution Numeric (radians); optional angular twist glue zone, passed fisheye_fgc(). target_crs Optional working CRS (anything accepted sf::st_crs() / sf::st_transform()). NULL, projected CRS auto-selected input lon/lat; otherwise input CRS used. preserve_aspect Logical. TRUE (default), use uniform scaling; FALSE, scale axes independently (may stretch shapes).

title: Radial fisheye warp for sf/sfc objects (auto-CRS + flexible centers) — sf_fisheye
text: object top-level class sf_obj (sf sfc), geometry coordinates warped fisheye original CRS restored.

title: Radial fisheye warp for sf/sfc objects (auto-CRS + flexible centers) — sf_fisheye
text: CRS handling. target_crs NULL input geographic (lon/lat), projected working CRS chosen layer’s centroid: Victoria, AU region (approximate 140–150°E, 40–30°S): EPSG:7855 (GDA2020 / MGA55). Otherwise UTM: EPSG:326## (north) EPSG:327## (south). may override target_crs. original CRS restored return. Center selection. fisheye center can supplied multiple ways: center = c(lon, lat), center_crs = "EPSG:4326" (recommended WGS84) another CRS string/object. center = c(x, y) already working CRS map units (meters). center sf/sfc geometry (POINT/LINE/POLYGON/etc.): centroid combined geometry used, transformed working CRS. center = c(cx, cy) normalized coordinates \([-1,1]\) normalized_center = TRUE (relative bbox midpoint scale used normalization). Legacy cx, cy (map units) still accepted used center supplied. Normalization. Let bbox half-width/height sx, sy. preserve_aspect = TRUE (default), uniform scale s = max(sx, sy) maps \((x, y) \mapsto ((x - cx)/s,\, (y - cy)/s)\), r_in/r_out (e.g., 0.34/0.5) interpreted unit-like space. preserve_aspect = FALSE, X Y independently scaled sx sy. Implementation notes. Geometry coordinates transformed st_transform_custom() safely re-closes polygon rings drops Z/M. radial warp delegated fisheye_fgc() (modified). transformation may introduce self-intersections topology issues due geometric warping.

code: library(sf)  # A simple coordinate transformer: scale and shift scale_shift <- function(coords, sx = 1, sy = 1, dx = 0, dy = 0) {  X <- coords[, 1] * sx + dx  Y <- coords[, 2] * sy + dy   cbind(X, Y) }  # POINT example pt <- st_sfc(st_point(c(0, 0)), crs = 3857) st_transform_custom(pt, transform_fun = scale_shift,                     args = list(sx = 2, sy = 2, dx = 1000, dy = -500)) #> Geometry set for 1 feature  #> Geometry type: POINT #> Dimension:     XY #> Bounding box:  xmin: 1000 ymin: -500 xmax: 1000 ymax: -500 #> Projected CRS: WGS 84 / Pseudo-Mercator #> POINT (1000 -500)  # LINESTRING example ln <- st_sfc(st_linestring(rbind(c(0, 0), c(1, 0), c(1, 1))), crs = 3857) st_transform_custom(ln, transform_fun = scale_shift,                     args = list(sx = 10, sy = 10)) #> Geometry set for 1 feature  #> Geometry type: LINESTRING #> Dimension:     XY #> Bounding box:  xmin: 0 ymin: 0 xmax: 10 ymax: 10 #> Projected CRS: WGS 84 / Pseudo-Mercator #> LINESTRING (0 0, 10 0, 10 10)  # POLYGON example (unit square) poly <- st_sfc(st_polygon(list(rbind(c(0,0), c(1,0), c(1,1),                                      c(0,1), c(0,0)))), crs = 3857) st_transform_custom(poly, transform_fun = scale_shift,                     args = list(sx = 2, sy = 0.5, dx = 5)) #> Geometry set for 1 feature  #> Geometry type: POLYGON #> Dimension:     XY #> Bounding box:  xmin: 0 ymin: 0 xmax: 1 ymax: 1 #> Projected CRS: WGS 84 / Pseudo-Mercator #> POLYGON ((0 0, 1 0, 1 1, 0 1, 0 0))  # MULTIPOLYGON example (two disjoint squares) mp <- st_sfc(st_multipolygon(list(   list(rbind(c(0,0), c(1,0), c(1,1), c(0,1), c(0,0))),   list(rbind(c(2,2), c(3,2), c(3,3), c(2,3), c(2,2))) )), crs = 3857) st_transform_custom(mp, transform_fun = scale_shift,                     args = list(dx = 100, dy = 100)) #> Geometry set for 1 feature  #> Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON #> Dimension:     XY #> Bounding box:  xmin: 100 ymin: 100 xmax: 103 ymax: 103 #> Projected CRS: WGS 84 / Pseudo-Mercator #> MULTIPOLYGON (((100 100, 101 100, 101 101, 100 ...  # In an sf data frame sf_df <- st_sf(id = 1:2, geometry = st_sfc(   st_point(c(10, 10)),   st_linestring(rbind(c(0,0), c(2,0), c(2,2))) ), crs = 3857)  st_transform_custom(sf_df, transform_fun = scale_shift,                     args = list(sx = 3, sy = 3)) #> Simple feature collection with 2 features and 1 field #> Geometry type: GEOMETRY #> Dimension:     XY #> Bounding box:  xmin: 0 ymin: 0 xmax: 30 ymax: 30 #> Projected CRS: WGS 84 / Pseudo-Mercator #>   id                   geometry #> 1  1              POINT (30 30) #> 2  2 LINESTRING (0 0, 6 0, 6 6)
